title: You Are Mine: Redeemed Witnesses and a New Exodus
summary: God tells Israel not to fear, because he created them, redeemed them, called them by name, and will be with them through water and fire. He gathers his scattered children from every direction and calls the blind and deaf people to be his witnesses in a courtroom where the nations' gods have nothing to say. He announces a new exodus from Babylon greater than the first, and then turns to Israel's sins, which he blots out for his own sake.
story: Chapter 42 ended with a hard verdict: Israel, God's servant, had been blind and deaf, and the exile was God's judgment. Chapter 43 opens with “Now,” and the tone changes completely. The same people who were handed over to plunderers are told “you are Mine.” The chapter holds together what the exiles most needed to hear: God has not given up on them, and their return from Babylon will be a new act of salvation, as decisive as the exodus from Egypt. Yet it also refuses to pretend they deserved it. The final section returns to their sin and grounds their future not in their faithfulness but in God's own name.
historical:
Verse 14 names Babylon and the Chaldeans, the people of southern Mesopotamia whose dynasty ruled the Neo-Babylonian Empire from Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar to its fall to Cyrus in 539 BC. The picture of the Chaldeans fleeing in the ships “in which they rejoice” reflects Babylon's position on the Euphrates and its web of canals and river trade, though the Hebrew of the line is difficult and translations vary.

The promise in verse 3 that God gives Egypt, Cush, and Seba as a ransom for Israel names peoples of northeast Africa: Egypt, Cush along the Nile to the south (roughly modern Sudan), and Seba, which Genesis 10:7 lists among the descendants of Cush. Many interpreters note that the Persian Empire that released the exiles went on to conquer Egypt under Cyrus's son Cambyses in 525 BC, though the verse is poetry and speaks broadly of God valuing Israel above the great nations.
cultural:
The first verse is full of the language of belonging. To call someone by name was to claim a relationship with them, as parents name children and owners marked property. To redeem, in Israelite law, was the act of a near relative who paid to free a family member or to recover family land. A ransom (kopher) was the price paid to release a life that was forfeit. The chapter uses all of these to say that Israel belongs to God as family, and that he will pay whatever is needed to get them back.

The courtroom language of verses 9 to 13 depends on the role of witnesses in ancient Israelite law, where cases were decided by the testimony of at least two witnesses. The nations have no witnesses for their gods; Israel, blind and deaf as it is, has seen what God has done and can testify. Verses 23 and 24 mention the materials of temple worship: sheep for burnt offerings, frankincense, and sweet cane, an aromatic reed imported at cost and used in the holy anointing oil (Exodus 30:23). In exile, with no temple, those offerings had ceased, but the chapter's charge is that Israel had wearied God with sin long before that.
literary: The chapter weaves together forms seen in chapters 41 and 42. It opens with an oracle of salvation (verses 1 to 7) built on “Do not fear” twice. A trial speech (verses 8 to 13) summons the nations and makes Israel God's witness. A second oracle (verses 14 to 21) announces the fall of Babylon and a new exodus, describing God as the one who made a way through the sea and then telling Israel not to dwell on the former things, because the new thing will outshine them. A final disputation (verses 22 to 28) turns the courtroom on Israel itself. Key words bind the chapter together: create and form, which appear at the start and in verse 21, and the emphatic “I, yes I” of verses 11 and 25, where the one who alone saves is also the one who alone blots out sin.

outline.t: Do not fear: created, redeemed, called, and gathered
Israel called as God's witnesses before the nations
Babylon's fall and a new exodus through the wilderness
Israel's weariness and sin, and God who blots it out

doctrines.note: “I, yes I, am the LORD, and there is no Savior but Me.” Salvation is God's work from first to last, and its ground is his own name: he blots out transgressions “for My own sake,” not because Israel has earned it.
The chapter is one of the Old Testament's clearest statements of monotheism: “Before Me no god was formed, and after Me none will come.” The LORD is not the greatest among gods but the only one.
Israel is chosen to be God's witness, formed so that it will “declare My praise.” Election is for testimony.
The new exodus looks ahead to a salvation greater than the first. “Behold, I am about to do something new.” Biblical hope remembers God's past acts in order to expect greater ones.

words.note: Ed, witness. In Israel's courts, a witness testified to what he had seen and heard. God calls his people “My witnesses” twice (verses 10 and 12). Their testimony is not an argument they invent but an account of what God has done among them.

Kopher, ransom, the price paid to release a life that would otherwise be forfeit, as in Exodus 21:30. Here God speaks of giving nations as Israel's ransom, stressing how precious his people are to him. The idea of a ransom paid for God's people becomes central to the New Testament.

Chadash, new. “I am about to do something new.” In these chapters the new thing is the return from Babylon, described as a new exodus. The word signals that God's saving history moves forward and is not merely a repetition of the past.

Machah, to wipe out or blot out, used of erasing writing from a scroll or wiping a dish clean. God is the one who blots out Israel's transgressions, removing the record against them, and remembers their sins no more.

christ: The chapter's language echoes through the New Testament in several ways. Jesus tells his disciples that they will be his witnesses to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8), taking up the role Israel is given here. First Peter 2:9 describes the church as a chosen people who proclaim God's excellencies, drawing on verses 20 and 21 alongside Exodus 19. Paul's words about the new creation in Christ, where the old has passed away and the new has come (2 Corinthians 5:17), echo verses 18 and 19. Jesus's repeated “I am He” sayings in John's Gospel (for example John 8:24) resemble God's words in verses 10 and 13, and the claim that there is no Savior besides the LORD becomes, in the New Testament, the confession that Jesus is Savior and Lord. Finally, the idea of a ransom paid for God's people is taken up by Jesus himself, who said he came to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). These are connections of theme and language, grounded in the New Testament's own use.

hard.q: How can God give other nations as a ransom for Israel? Does he value some peoples above others?
hard.a:
The line is jarring to a modern reader, and it should be taken seriously. Most interpreters read it as poetic hyperbole in the language of the ransom price: God is saying that he would pay anything, even the greatest kingdoms of the day, to recover his people. It is a statement of how precious Israel is to him, not a policy of sacrificing others. Some also connect it historically to the Persian Empire, which released Israel and later conquered Egypt, as though the Persians were given Egypt in exchange for letting Israel go.

The wider context matters too. The same chapters insist that the nations are invited to share in God's salvation (42:6; 45:22; 49:6) and that Israel was chosen to be a light to them. Israel's election is not favoritism but vocation. Readers who find the verse troubling can note that the book itself holds together God's particular love for his people and his intention to bless every nation through them.

questions: God says “I have called you by your name; you are Mine.” What difference does it make to you to be known and claimed by name?
The promise is not that there will be no waters or fire, but that God will be with his people in them. How have you experienced that difference?
God tells Israel not to dwell on the former things. What past, good or bad, might be keeping you from seeing what God is doing now?
